programme: VDR, the vitamin-D nuclear receptor, and CREBBP (CBP), its histone-acetyltransferase coactivator, form the canonical liganded-nuclear-receptor/coactivator pair: VDR (heterodimerized with RXR, not in this list) docks its AF-2 surface onto CBP, whose HAT activity opens chromatin at VDR response elements so VDR target genes (e.g. CDKN1B, RARB, CYP24A1, CCND3, EGFR in the target list) get transcribed.
role_in_a: VDR signalling in brain tissue is reported to modulate mitochondrial/neuronal dynamics, amyloid pathology and treatment response by genotype; CREBBP is required for CREB-dependent transcription implicated in AD-associated biomarker networks — i.e. the module is invoked as a protective, differentiation/plasticity-maintaining transcriptional axis whose failure tracks with neurodegeneration.
role_in_b: VDR is described as a broadly tumor-modulating nuclear receptor in GI cancer, with receptor levels/polymorphisms tied to gastric cancer risk and outcome; CREBBP is recurrently mutated in its HAT/bromodomains in GI cancers, driving hypermutation and stratifying survival, and is used in molecular subtyping of gastric adenocarcinoma — i.e. loss or alteration of the same coactivator relationship is tumor-promoting rather than protective.
shared_axis: Because CREBBP is the coactivator VDR needs to convert ligand binding into an open-chromatin transcriptional event, any tissue that relies on VDR-driven differentiation/homeostatic gene expression is exposed to the same bottleneck when CREBBP is limiting or mutated; that would explain why the identical VDR–CREBBP pairing shows up as a protective axis in brain (its failure permits neurodegeneration) and as a tumor-suppressive/mutational-target axis in stomach (its failure permits hypermutation and dedifferentiation), without requiring the two tissues to share lineage or cell type.
reasoning: Both VDR and CREBBP are independently placed by multiple retrieved papers in Alzheimer's disease AND in stomach cancer, and the module itself (liganded nuclear receptor plus its CBP coactivator) is a textbook, nameable mechanism rather than a post-hoc grouping. No retrieved paper connects the two diseases directly through this axis, which caps the verdict at 'supported' rather than 'established.'
support: PMID 41335161 — VDR ortholog Hr96 modulates neuronal/mitochondrial dynamics in a Drosophila AD model; PMID 41910814 — vitamin D3/VDR attenuates AD-like amyloid pathology; PMID 39112893 — VDR genotype affects rivastigmine response in AD patients; PMID 41527579 — review of VDR biological functions and mechanisms in cancer; PMID 40784088 — VDR gene polymorphisms associated with GI (incl. gastric) cancer; PMID 42009747 — CREBBP among SUMO-related biomarker genes in AD networks; PMID 40671224 — CREBBP implicated in AD mechanism/network analysis; PMID 41301688 — CREBBP/EP300 HAT and bromodomain mutations drive hypermutation and predict survival in GI cancer; PMID 41232140 — CREBBP included in molecular profiling of gastric adenocarcinoma subtypes.
how_to_falsify: In parallel calcitriol-stimulated gastric epithelial and neuronal/microglial cell models, knock down CREBBP and ChIP for CBP occupancy plus qPCR induction of shared VDR targets (e.g. CYP24A1, CDKN1B); if CREBBP loss fails to blunt VDR-driven transcription in either tissue, or CBP is not recruited to VDR-bound loci, the shared-coactivator-bottleneck account is falsified.
caveats: Brain and stomach share no developmental lineage, so any connection is coactivator-based, not anatomical; findings are aggregated over 240 patient-group comparisons across only 3 independent cohort pairs, and VDR (65%) and CREBBP (63%) recur less often than TFAP2A, ZBTB10 or FOSL1, which were left out here only because no retrieved paper places them in both diseases. NR3C1, another CBP-client nuclear receptor, was excluded as tissue-generic — its absence reflects that filter, not an oversight, and the account should be read as specific to VDR/CREBBP recurrence rather than 'any nuclear receptor.' Several other factors' additional papers could not be judged from the text available, so their silence on a cross-disease link is a retrieval gap, not evidence against one.
